name: Domesday Book
info: Domesday Book is the manuscript record of the Great Survey of much of England and parts of Wales, ordered by William the Conqueror and traditionally dated to 1086, and a primary source for English economic history.

facts.made: Ordered by William the Conqueror in 1085; returns gathered by royal officers (legati) from sworn juries; Great Domesday copied out by one scribe, Little Domesday by about six
facts.form: A survey in highly abbreviated Medieval Latin on parchment, in two works: Little Domesday (Norfolk, Suffolk and Essex) and Great Domesday (most of the rest of England and parts of Wales)
facts.where: The National Archives at Kew, London
facts.known: the oldest public record of England; 268,984 heads of household tallied; 13,418 places named; 5,624 mills listed; a name alluding to the Last Judgment; evidence still cited in courts

t: The survey recorded who held each piece of land after the Norman Conquest, what it was worth and what dues the king was owed.
Its date is traditionally 1086, but some historians argue that the book itself was compiled later, under William II or as late as 1098 to 1114.
Kept first at Winchester and then at Westminster, it is now at the National Archives and was printed in full in 1783.
dyk: The English called it Domesday because, as Richard FitzNeal explained around 1179, there was no appeal from its record, just as there is none from the Last Judgment. The word doom then meant law or judgment, not disaster.
ev: According to the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, William the Conqueror sends his men into every shire to survey the land and its dues
The book's colophon states that the survey was completed
Richard FitzNeal explains the name Domesday in the Dialogus de Scaccario
The name Domesday is first found in an official document
Domesday is first printed in full, in two volumes set in record type
The two volumes are transferred to the new Public Record Office in London
During the Second World War the volumes are evacuated to Shepton Mallet Prison in Somerset
The volumes are rebound for the ninth centenary, and the BBC releases the Domesday Project

sections.origins:
Domesday Book came out of the years after the Norman Conquest, when William the Conqueror had confiscated landed estates across England on a large scale and given them to his followers. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle states that in 1085 the king held a large meeting and deep consultation with his council about the land, how it was occupied and by what sort of men, and then sent his men into every shire to find out how many hides each held, what land and stock the king had, and what dues he ought to receive each year.

Historians believe William needed to show that the rights of the Crown, which he claimed to have inherited, had not suffered in the confiscations, since his Norman followers tended to evade the liabilities of their English predecessors. The primary purpose of the survey was to record the king's fiscal rights: the national land tax (geld), paid on a fixed assessment, certain other dues, and the proceeds of the crown lands. The framework for the book was the geld assessment lists, which is why the northern lands that paid no geld were largely left out. The manuscript was first known as Liber de Wintonia, the Book of Winchester, after the royal treasury where it was kept.
sections.content:
Domesday Book is made up of two independent works. Little Domesday, physically smaller but more detailed, covers Norfolk, Suffolk and Essex and records the livestock on lords' home farms. Great Domesday covers most of the rest of England and parts of Wales, but not the northern lands that later became Westmorland, Cumberland, Northumberland and the County Palatine of Durham. Space was left in it for London and Winchester, which were never written up.

Each volume is arranged in chapters listing the manors held by each tenant-in-chief directly from the king, opening with the king's own demesne, then bishops, abbeys, lay tenants-in-chief and lastly the king's serjeants and thegns. For each manor the record gives the tax assessment, the arable land and plough teams, meadow, woodland, pasture, fisheries, mills and salt-pans, the peasants by class, and the annual value at the death of Edward the Confessor, when the new holder received it and at the time of the survey. In all it tallies 268,984 heads of household, names 13,418 places and lists 5,624 mills and 28,000 slaves; H. C. Darby put the total population at between 1.2 and 1.6 million.
sections.making:
Most shires were visited by a group of royal officers (legati) who held a public inquiry, probably in the shire court, attended by representatives of every township and of the local lords. The unit of inquiry was the hundred, and each hundred's return was sworn to by 12 local jurors, half English and half Norman. Comparison of the details recorded suggests six circuits for Great Domesday and a seventh for the Little Domesday shires. Fuller records of the original returns survive in the Cambridge Inquisition, the Inquisitio Eliensis of Ely Abbey and the Exon Domesday for the south-western counties.

Great Domesday appears to have been copied out on parchment by one person, while six scribes seem to have worked on Little Domesday, which represents an earlier stage before the drastic abbreviation and rearrangement of the Great Domesday scribe. It is not known exactly when the book was compiled. Writing in 2000, David Roffe argued that the inquest and the making of the book were distinct exercises and that the book was completed, if not started, by William II; research by Carol Symes indicates it might have been completed as late as 1098 to 1114.
sections.reception:
To the English, who held the book in awe, it became known as Domesday, in allusion to the Last Judgment and to the definitive character of the record. Richard FitzNeal, treasurer of England under Henry II, wrote in the Dialogus de Scaccario (c. 1179) that when any dispute arose about matters in the book, its word could not be denied or set aside, so that from it, as from the Last Judgment, there was no appeal. The custodians took up the name, first found in an official document in 1221. Through false etymology or wordplay it was also linked with the Latin Domus Dei, a reading found in Adam of Damerham in the late 13th century and believed by antiquaries such as John Stow and Sir Richard Baker.

In the Middle Ages the book's evidence was frequently invoked in the law courts. Early British authors thought the survey's aim was to show that all private property in land came only from the grant of King William. Around 1100 the Normans in southern Italy completed their own Catalogus Baronum based on Domesday Book. The usual modern convention calls the work Domesday Book, without a definite article.
sections.survival:
The book was kept from the late 11th to the early 13th century in the royal Treasury at Winchester, and went with the Treasury to the Palace of Westminster, probably under King John. It stayed at Westminster in various Exchequer offices until the 19th century, apart from journeys with the Chancellor of the Exchequer to York and Lincoln in 1300, to York in 1303 and 1319, to Hertford in the 1580s or 1590s and to Nonsuch Palace in 1666 after the Great Fire of London. From the 1740s it was held in the chapter house of Westminster Abbey, and in 1859 it moved to the new Public Record Office.

The volumes have been rebound many times: Little Domesday in 1320, both probably in the Tudor period, in 1819 and 1869, in 1952 and in 1986, when Great Domesday was divided into two physical volumes and Little Domesday into three. They were sent to Southampton in 1861 to 1863 for photozincographic reproduction, and evacuated to Bodmin Prison during the First World War and to Shepton Mallet Prison during the Second World War. They are now held at the National Archives at Kew, together with the chest in which they were stowed in the 17th and 18th centuries.
sections.legacy:
The government began a project to publish Domesday in 1773, and the book appeared in two volumes in 1783, set in record type as a partial facsimile; indexes followed in 1811 and a supplementary volume with the Exon Domesday, the Inquisitio Eliensis, the Liber Winton and the Boldon Book in 1816. Photographic facsimiles of each county were published in 1861 to 1863. In 1986 the BBC marked the 900th anniversary with its Domesday Project, and in 2006 the contents went online with an English translation.

No survey approaching its scope was attempted again in Britain until the 1873 Return of Owners of Land, sometimes called the Modern Domesday. The book is a primary source for historians, especially economic historians; H. C. Darby called it the oldest public record in England and probably the most remarkable statistical document in the history of Europe. Darby also warned of its omissions, errors and ambiguities, and of the difference between the geography of England and the geography of Domesday Book. Its evidence has still been cited in courts in recent decades, on manorial rights in 1960 and 2010 and on a market in 2019.

summary: Domesday Book is the record of the Great Survey of England ordered by William the Conqueror in 1085, listing who held the land, its resources and its value to the king. Traditionally dated to 1086, though some historians date the book later, it is held at the National Archives and remains a primary source for medieval England.
